title: Information Technology Rules, 2021
text:
During Monsoon session of the Parliament in 2018 a motion on “Misuse of social media platforms and spreading of fake news” was admitted. The Minister of Electronics and Information Technology accordingly made a detailed statement of the "resolve of the Government to strengthen the legal framework and make the social media platforms accountable under the law". MeitY then prepared the draft Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines) Rules 2018 to replace the 2022 rules.[1] The Information Technology Act, 2000 provided that intermediaries are protected liabilities in some cases.[2] The draft 2018 Rules sought to elaborate the liabilities and responsibilities of the intermediaries in a better way.[2] Further the draft Rules have been made "in order to prevent spreading of fake news, curb obscene information on the internet, prevent misuse of social-media platforms and to provide security to the users."[2] The move followed a notice issued to WhatsApp in July 2018, warning it against helping to spread fake news and look on as a "mute spectator".[3]

In relation to the Prajawala case, on 11 December 2018, the Supreme Court of India observed that "the Government of India may frame the necessary Guidelines / SOP and implement them within two weeks so as to eliminate child pornography, rape and gang rape imageries, videos and sites in content hosting platforms and other applications." Further a parliamentary report laid in 2020 studied the effect of pornography on children.[4,5]

On 5 January 2019 a government open house was held to discuss the Rules.[6] Further, ten days were given for counter comments, until 28 January.[7] On 21 September 2019 the Centre informed the Madras High Court bench under Justice M Sathyanarayanan that deliberations on the Draft Rules 2018 had been completed.[8] Facebook wrote a plea to transfer the matter to the Supreme Court.[8,9]

MeitY had invited comments on proposed amendments early in 2019. The amendments were seen by many to "overstep the aforesaid intention sparking concerns of violating free speech and privacy rights of individuals."[10] It is seen that "the guidelines suffer with excessive delegation of powers and shift the burden of responsibility of identification of unlawful content from a government/ judiciary to intermediaries."[11] A total of 171 comments were received by MeitY; all of the comments were published for counter comments.[12,13] On 21 October 2019, MeitY asked the court for three months’ time for finalisation of the Intermediary Rules, 2018.[12]
